items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism give different answers
items.claim: What is the distinction between act and rule utilitarianism?

options.text: They are alternative names for the same theory

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences directly; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would produce the greatest happiness — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to maximise utility differently
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R.M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.

items.title: Nicaea was a political project as much as a theological one
items.claim: Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE. What was his primary motive?

options.text: Pure theological inquiry into the nature of Christ
Political unity — the empire had recently legalised Christianity, and the Arian controversy was fracturing the church
To remove gospels he personally disliked from the Bible
To suppress the worship of Mary

items.reveal:
Constantine had legalised Christianity by the Edict of Milan (313). The Arian controversy (was the Son co-eternal with the Father, or created?) threatened civil order. Constantine wrote to Bishop Alexander and Arius effectively telling them to stop arguing.

The Council produced the Nicene Creed and condemned Arius. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 — by an Arian bishop. Theological disputes continued for decades; Athanasius was exiled five times.

The Council did NOT decide the canon of Scripture (a persistent Dan Brown myth).
items.why: Doctrines aren't formed in a vacuum. Constantine wanted a workable state religion. The metaphysics of the Trinity took shape under that pressure — neither invalidating it nor making it 'pure theology'.

items.title: Buddhism has no creator god
items.claim: Does Buddhism teach the existence of a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is the supreme deity worshipped as such
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana Buddhism affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher.
items.why: Western religious frameworks define 'religion' through theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.
